title: How Science Stays Honest
text: Notice how careful the scientists had to be. That caution is the heart of good science, because a tempting story can still be wrong.

title: How Science Stays Honest
text: The goal is not to find an exciting answer. The goal is to find an answer that survives every test you can think of.

title: How Science Stays Honest
text: Finding iridium did not prove anything by itself. It was a clue, and a clue is not a conviction.

title: How Science Stays Honest
text: A good investigator asks what else must be true if the story is right.
nxt: If an enormous object really struck the planet, then somewhere on Earth there should be a scar.

text: Later studies confirmed a buried impact crater called Chicxulub, stretching more than one hundred and fifty kilometers wide.
nxt: Its age matched the iridium layer closely, and it felt like the missing piece of a puzzle sliding into place.

title: The Impact
text: Imagine a mountain of rock roughly ten to fifteen kilometers across, traveling at tens of thousands of kilometers per hour.
nxt: When it slammed into a shallow sea, the energy released was comparable to billions of atomic bombs detonating all at once.

text: Rock vaporized instantly, and scientists estimate that the blow carved a cavity deeper than the crust is thick.
nxt: Can you fathom the sheer scale of such a blow?

title: The Impact
text: Earthquakes shook the planet, and towering tsunamis swept across the ocean, leaving traces in rocks far from the crater.

title: A Mountain Meets the Ground
text: Try to hold that moment in your mind, and be honest about how little our ordinary experience prepares us for it.
nxt: A mountain of rock bigger than the tallest peaks on Earth, moving faster than any bullet.

title: A Mountain Meets the Ground
text: Nothing in everyday life moves like that. When something that large and that fast meets the ground, the rock behaves almost like a liquid for a moment.

title: A Mountain Meets the Ground
text: That is why the crater ended up so wide, and why the effects reached so far.

title: Billions of Bombs
text: Notice the comparison scientists reach for here. Billions of atomic bombs is not a literal description of a machine.

title: Billions of Bombs
text: It is a way to help the mind grasp an amount of energy that has no everyday equivalent.
nxt: We use such comparisons because the real numbers are too large to feel.

title: Glass Rain and Fire
text: The true horror did not stop with the initial blast. Vast amounts of vaporized and melted rock were thrown high above the atmosphere.

title: Glass Rain and Fire
text: As these tiny droplets of molten glass rained back down across the globe, friction with the air made them glow.

title: Glass Rain and Fire
text: Many scientists think the heat from that rain turned the sky into something like an oven, and that fires broke out across large parts of the world.
nxt: How could any creature survive when the sky itself felt like a furnace?

title: A Chain of Disasters
text: Here the story changes from a single blow into a chain of events.

title: A Chain of Disasters
text: This was not one disaster. It was a chain of them, each one setting up the next.

title: The Cold and the Dark
text: After the fires came the cold.
nxt: Soot from burning forests, mixed with sulfur released from vaporized rock on the seafloor, likely formed a thick haze that blocked out the sun.

title: The Cold and the Dark
text: Models suggest the world lived in a freezing twilight for years. With little sunlight reaching the soil, how could the plants endure?

title: The Cold and the Dark
text: Photosynthesis slowed or stopped across land and oceans, and the base of the food chain shattered.
nxt: Giant herbivores likely starved first, followed by the hunters that depended on them.

title: The World After the Fires
text: Now imagine the world after the fires. The sky is gray and thick with soot.

title: The World After the Fires
text: The sun is a dim smear, if you can see it at all. For years the days feel like twilight.

title: The World After the Fires
text: Plants need sunlight to make food, so when the light fails, the green things on land and the tiny floating plants in the sea stop working.

title: Why Giants Fell
text: This is why the biggest animals were in such danger. A giant needs an enormous amount of food every day.

title: Why Giants Fell
text: When the plants fail, the plant eaters starve first, and the hunters that depended on them soon follow.
nxt: Being huge, which had been a triumph for so long, became a trap.

title: Why Giants Fell
text: It is a hard lesson from deep time: the very thing that makes a species powerful in good times can make it fragile when the world changes suddenly.

title: Was the Asteroid Alone?
text: Was the asteroid striking a healthy planet alone, or was Earth already under strain?
nxt: Geologists have found evidence of colossal volcanic eruptions in what is now India, forming the massive Deccan Traps.

title: Why the Debate Matters
text: Scientists agree that the asteroid struck, and the crater under the Gulf of Mexico is the proof.
nxt: What everyone accepts is that the combination of crises was catastrophic for life.

title: Why the Debate Matters
text: And why does this debate matter? Because it changes how we think about extinction.

title: Why the Debate Matters
text: If the impact alone did it, then the dinosaurs were healthy and simply unlucky.
nxt: If the volcanoes had already weakened the world, then the asteroid may have been the final push on a planet under strain.

title: Why the Debate Matters
text: Either way, a living world can be fragile in ways that are hard to see until something goes wrong.

title: Who Could Endure?
text: Who could endure a planet stripped of light and warmth? In this dark and broken world, being large and powerful was no longer an advantage.

title: Who Could Endure?
text: The survivors were not the giant monsters with razor-sharp teeth, but modest creatures.
nxt: Small mammals that could burrow underground, animals that could feed on dead plants and animals, and small birds managed to scrape by.

title: Who Could Endure?
text: When the sunlight finally returned, the reign of the non-avian dinosaurs was permanently over.

title: Who Lived
text: Let us look closely at who lived. Survival was not about strength.

title: Who Lived
text: It was about being small, about being able to hide, and about being able to live on whatever was left.
nxt: A creature that could burrow underground could wait out the worst of the heat and the cold.

title: Standing in the Aftermath
text: Today, as you drink your morning coffee or walk along a crowded city sidewalk, you are standing on the other side of that ancient event.

title: Standing in the Aftermath
text: When the reign of the great reptiles ended, the world opened up for small mammals that had been living in their shadow, and their descendants include us.

title: Standing in the Aftermath
text: We often tell the history of life as if it were moving toward us, step by step. But this chapter suggests something humbler.

title: Standing in the Aftermath
text: The path of life can turn on one unlikely event, and a stray asteroid may be part of the reason we are here to ask about it.

title: A Sparrow on a Branch
text: The story of the dinosaurs is not merely an ancient tragedy. It is also a testament to the resilience of life.

title: A Sparrow on a Branch
text: Even beneath a blanket of ash and darkened skies, life endured, and it slowly rebuilt a living world.

title: A Sparrow on a Branch
text: And it leaves us with a quiet question to carry outside: if one stray rock from space could rewrite the history of Earth,
nxt: what else have the stones beneath our feet been waiting to tell us?
